title: MUSS-TI: Multi-level Shuttle Scheduling for Large-Scale Entanglement Module Linked Trapped-Ion
problem: Compiling quantum circuits for Entanglement Module Linked Quantum Charge-Coupled Device (EML-QCCD) trapped-ion architectures is inefficient because existing compilers do not account for the distinct functional zones (storage, operation, optical/entanglement) within each QCCD module, leading to excessive ion shuttle operations and reduced circuit fidelity. Cross-module nonlocal gates via photonic fiber links further complicate qubit routing.
method: MUSS-TI constructs a dependency graph (DAG) of the quantum circuit and applies a multi-level scheduling strategy analogous to classical memory scheduling: storage zones map to L0 (disk), operation zones to L1 (memory), and optical zones to L2 (CPU). Gate selection prioritizes immediately executable gates; qubit routing assigns each qubit to the nearest-level available zone; conflict handling uses an LRU eviction policy to relocate the least-recently-used qubit to a lower-level zone. A look-ahead SWAP insertion algorithm (k=8 layers) strategically inserts SWAP gates between different QCCD modules to reduce long-range shuttle counts; a SABRE-inspired bidirectional initial mapping further reduces overhead.

title: Past-Future Scheduler for LLM Serving under SLA Guarantees
problem: LLM serving frameworks using continuous batching suffer from either overestimation of memory consumption (conservative schedulers) or underestimation leading to harmful request evictions (aggressive schedulers), because neither accurately accounts for the dynamic memory release profile of concurrently running requests across future decoding steps.
method: The Past-Future scheduler combines two components: (1) output length distribution prediction that samples predicted output lengths from the empirical distribution of recent historical requests (a sliding window of ~1,000 finished requests), updating each running request's predicted remaining length at every decode step using the conditional distribution P(l > l_current); and (2) future required memory estimation that sorts running requests by estimated remaining length, computes memory occupancy at each future completion event, and determines peak future memory as max(M_t+1, M_t+2, ...) across all future completion times. A queued request is admitted only if adding it keeps peak future memory below hardware capacity. This is implemented in LightLLM with <1% scheduling overhead using GPU-parallel computation.

title: Formalising CXL Cache Coherence
problem: The CXL.cache inter-device cache coherence protocol specification (governing coherence between CPUs, GPUs, and accelerators over PCIe) contains ambiguities, redundancies, inaccuracies, and potential coherence violations that could cause incompatible vendor implementations or incorrect hardware if left unresolved.
method: The authors formalize CXL.cache as a state-transition system in the Isabelle proof assistant, modeling 20 system components (device caches, host cache, message channels, buffers, programs, transaction counter) and 68 transition rules encoding the complete legal message flows. They perform scenario verification (litmus tests from CXL message-sequence charts) to validate model faithfulness and to show that relaxing restrictions such as Snoop-pushes-GO causes coherence violations. They then prove the Single-Writer-Multiple-Reader (SWMR) property by constructing a 796-conjunct inductive invariant that implies SWMR and is preserved by all 68 rules (53,332 lemmas), using a custom super_sketch Isabelle automation tool to manage proof scale.

title: Finesse: An Agile Design Framework for Pairing-based Cryptography via Software/Hardware Co-Design
problem: Pairing-based cryptography (PBC) accelerators require frequent re-engineering as security demands grow and pairing curve parameters evolve, but existing designs are either highly customized (inflexible) or flexible but low-performance, with no framework automating the algorithm-to-hardware translation across diverse pairing curves. The complex interdependency among algorithm choices, finite-field operator variants, and hardware configurations makes design-space exploration intractable manually.
method: Finesse introduces a three-layer abstraction: an intermediate representation (IR) for finite-field operations over arbitrary extension fields, a RISC-flavor Fp-level ISA with VLIW extension, and a parameterized hardware pipeline model. A specialized compiler performs SSA-based dataflow optimization, instruction scheduling with issue-slot affinity optimization, and register bank allocation before generating binary for target hardware. A cycle-accurate simulator enables co-design feedback loops with EDA toolchain synthesis metrics. The hardware implements modular arithmetic ALUs (mmul, madd, mlin, minv) in a multi-core SIMT architecture with shared instruction memory on ASIC (40 nm) and FPGA (Virtex-7) platforms.

title: Flexing RISC-V Instruction Subset Processors to Extreme Edge
problem: Extreme edge applications (smart labels, wearable healthcare, smart textiles) require processors that are ultra-low area, ultra-low power, conformable, and low-cost—properties that conventional silicon RISC-V processors and existing smallest designs like Serv cannot meet—while still supporting programmability for occasional firmware updates.
method: The paper proposes RISC-V Instruction Subset Processors (RISSPs), generated by an automated methodology that (1) compiles applications to the full RV32E ISA to identify the required instruction subset (typically 24-86% of the ISA), (2) pulls formally pre-verified instruction hardware blocks from a library where each RISC-V instruction is implemented as a standalone, fully verified RTL block, (3) stitches them into a Modular Execution Unit (ModularEX) via a case-statement switch, and (4) synthesizes the result with commercial EDA tools (Synopsys ICC2 or Cadence Innovus) on Pragmatic Semiconductor's 0.6-um IGZO FlexIC process, where synthesis tools automatically eliminate redundant gates. A single-cycle non-pipelined microarchitecture suffices for kHz-range extreme edge performance requirements. For long-lasting applications needing firmware updates, a generative AI tool rewrites instructions not in the subset using equivalent subset instructions.
